extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in social psychology, statesmen/legislators, historians, students of crowd behaviour
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying descriptive criteria for recognizing and interpreting the psychological characteristics, causes, and consequences of crowds as set out in Gustave Le Bon's The Crowd. Useful for analysis, policy, or historical interpretation of mass behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological Law of the Mental Unity of Crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: When individuals are transformed into an organised (psychological) crowd, 'the sentiments and ideas of all the persons in the gathering take one and the same direction, and their conscious personality vanishes.' A collective mind is formed with clearly defined characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central rule: identify when a group shows unified sentiments/thoughts and disappearance of individual personality; only then treat it as a psychological crowd rather than an accidental aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Psychological Crowd (not mere aggregation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A numerically strong agglomeration does not suffice to form a crowd: to acquire 'special characteristics of psychological crowds' certain predisposing causes and a turning of ideas/sentiments in a definite direction are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between accidental gatherings and organised/psychological crowds. Look for purposeful orientation, common emotions or goals rather than mere co-location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical presence not required for crowd-psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Thousands of isolated individuals or an entire nation may acquire the characteristics of a psychological crowd under the influence of certain violent or intense emotions—even without visible agglomeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing mass behaviour, consider distributed phenomena (shared emotions, nation-wide fervour) as possible psychological crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of New Collective Characteristics (not averaging)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a crowd there is not a mere summing-up or average of individual traits; rather a combination occurs that creates new properties (analogy: chemical combination forming a new body with different properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not predict crowd behaviour by averaging member attributes; expect emergent properties and qualitatively different outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predominance of the Unconscious over Conscious Reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious phenomena preponderate; 'the conscious life of the mind is of small importance in comparison with its unconscious life.' Crowds bring to the fore the common, hereditary, unconscious substratum (the 'genius of a race').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect crowd actions to be driven by deep-seated collective sentiments and instincts rather than deliberative, reasoned argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowering of Intelligence and Weakening of Individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: In crowds intellectual aptitudes and individuality are weakened; 'in crowds it is stupidity and not mother-wit that is accumulated.' Crowds cannot accomplish acts demanding a high degree of intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat collective decisions as likely to reflect mediocre, common traits rather than expert reasoning; avoid overestimating crowds' capacity for complex deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and Loss of Responsibility (numerical sentiment of power)
rubrics_metrics.description: By numerical considerations an individual in a crowd acquires a sentiment of invincible power and, because a crowd is anonymous and therefore irresponsible, the sentiment of responsibility disappears, making individuals yield to instincts they would otherwise restrain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing likelihood of impulsive or antisocial acts, weigh the effects of perceived anonymity and collective empowerment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contagion (emotional and behavioural spread)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contagion is the phenomenon by which 'in a crowd every sentiment and act is contagious'—a hypnotic-order effect where emotions and actions spread rapidly among members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify mechanisms and channels of contagion (speech, gesture, demonstration) and anticipate rapid amplification of emotions/acts once contagion begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestibility / Hypnotic-like State
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals immersed in a crowd may enter a state resembling hypnosis: 'the conscious personality has entirely vanished; will and discernment are lost' and the crowd-member obeys collective suggestions, sometimes acting against prior character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize signals of suggestibility (reduced deliberation, imitation, obedience to leaders/gestures) and that leaders' suggestions can override individual moral or intellectual restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity Strengthens Suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggestion common to all members of a crowd gains strength by reciprocity; because the suggestion is shared, its force is amplified compared with the individual hypnotised subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor reinforcement dynamics: repeated, uniform messages/symbols will become disproportionately influential in a crowd context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance by Impressions and Sentiments, Not by Pure Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are not led by 'rules based on theories of pure equity' but by what produces an impression and seduces them; practical outcomes often follow impressions rather than logical justice (example: preference for indirect taxes that go unnoticed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When communicating with or designing policy for masses, emphasize impressions and perceptions (visibility, framing), since abstract rational arguments have limited effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick to Act but Poorly Adapted to Reasoning / Forethought
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are 'little adapted to reasoning' yet 'quick to act.' They lack the foresight required for complex economic procedures and are ill-equipped to execute disciplined, long-term constructive projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect rapid action but limited capacity for sustained, rational planning; policy responses should account for short-term impulsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds More Powerful for Destruction than for Creation
rubrics_metrics.description: History shows crowds primarily effect the dissolution of decayed civilisations; 'civilisations as yet have only been created and directed by a small intellectual aristocracy, never by crowds.' Crowds' rule tends toward a 'barbarian phase.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mass movements for destructive potential, especially where institutions are weakened; be cautious about relying on crowds for constructive institution-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous Crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological crowds are susceptible of classification: homogeneous crowds (sects, castes, classes) differ from heterogeneous crowds in particular characteristics that modify their mental constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment crowds by composition to predict differing behaviours; homogeneous crowds may show stronger unified responses aligned with shared traits, while heterogeneous crowds present other dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Importance for Legislators and Statesmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of crowd psychology is essential practice: it explains why laws and institutions have limited effect on crowds and why statesmen must seek what produces an impression on them rather than rely on abstract equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should use crowd-psychology-informed strategies (framing, symbolic actions, indirect measures) to influence mass behaviour and avoid naive appeals to pure reason.
